graph_team_stat_cfb_offense_replacement_.plain_summary: College football only. Swapping just the offensive EPA-per-play stat for a schedule-graph version that adjusts for opponent strength left the picks a shade better -- about three hundredths of a percentage point. It is the one arm of this experiment that came out on the favourable side, and it is small enough to be noise.

Swapping just the offensive success-rate stat for a schedule-graph version made the picks about a third of a percentage point worse when graded against the opening line, though it was a shade better against the closing line. graph_team_stat_cfb_offense_replacement_.plain_summary: College football only. We took the two offensive efficiency stats out of the model and replaced them with schedule-graph versions of the same stats that adjust for who each team played. Doing both at once made the picks slightly worse rather than better, by about a fifth of a percentage point, but the margin is small enough that it could still go either way.

graph_team_stat_cfb_offense_replacement_.plain_summary: College football only. After stripping both offensive stats out of the model, adding back schedule-graph versions of them was worth about a tenth of a percentage point LESS than adding nothing at all. Asked one stat at a time in an earlier study this same comparison looked favourable, so the joint version is the one that did not hold up.
